raw_text:
Transcaval access is a fully percutaneous, transfemoral venous route to the abdominal aorta that was developed to preserve the advantages of retrograde transcatheter structural intervention when iliofemoral arterial access is prohibitive. Its clinical niche emerged from the evolution of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR): after the first-in-human experience and pivotal trials established TAVR for inoperable, high-risk, and later low-risk aortic stenosis patients, vascular access became a major determinant of procedural feasibility and complications [1-7]. Although transfemoral TAVR is now dominant, hostile iliofemoral anatomy—small caliber vessels, circumferential calcification, tortuosity, prior stents, occlusion, or severe peripheral arterial disease—continues to require alternative strategies. Standardized endpoint definitions and CT-based screening have been essential for comparing access-related bleeding, vascular complications, and neurologic events across approaches [8-10].

The transcaval concept is counterintuitive but physiologically sound. A guidewire is advanced from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta using radiofrequency or electrosurgical energy, typically toward a prepositioned aortic snare. After wire externalization and tract dilation, a large-bore sheath is passed from femoral vein to IVC, through the retroperitoneal space, and into the aorta, permitting conventional retrograde TAVR delivery. The access tract is then closed with a nitinol occluder, with balloon tamponade or covered-stent bailout available if needed. Preclinical work demonstrated that arterial bleeding preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure cava rather than expanding catastrophically in the retroperitoneum [11]. The initial human TAVR series showed procedural feasibility in patients otherwise lacking acceptable access, with spontaneous closure of most residual aortocaval fistulas [12].

Careful CT planning is the cornerstone of safe transcaval access. The operator must identify a right-sided, calcium-free aortic window adjacent to the IVC, avoid interposed bowel or critical venous/arterial structures, ensure adequate distance from renal arteries and the aortoiliac bifurcation for occluder deployment and covered-stent bailout, and confirm that sheath length will provide secure intra-aortic purchase [13,14]. The technique has also been adapted to challenging anatomy, including traversal of a polyester aortic graft [15]. Contemporary procedural descriptions emphasize coaxial crossing, avoiding excessive traction on the snared wire, maintaining sheath position, full anticoagulation during large-bore access, reversal before closure when appropriate, and having bailout balloons, covered stents, and imaging support immediately available [16,17]. Laser-assisted crossing has been reported as an alternative when standard electrosurgical traversal is difficult [18].

Prospective evidence remains nonrandomized but informative. In the multicenter NHLBI transcaval TAVR investigation, transcaval access was successful in 99 of 100 attempted cases and device success was high, although bleeding and vascular complication rates reflected the extreme-risk population and early learning curve [19]. Twelve-month follow-up of the same cohort was reassuring: there were no late vascular complications directly attributable to transcaval access, and most fistulas were occluded on CT [20]. These data support the principle that a residual early aortocaval shunt is often benign, but persistent shunting may matter in patients with severe right heart dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, or limited ability to tolerate left-to-right flow.

Comparative evidence suggests that transcaval access is best considered among extrathoracic alternatives rather than alongside older transthoracic routes. Intrathoracic transapical and transaortic access have declined because of greater pain, pulmonary compromise, bleeding, and mortality. Transaxillary/subclavian and transcarotid access are now common alternatives, but they introduce arterial-dissection, bleeding, brachial plexus, internal mammary graft, and neurologic considerations. In a contemporary propensity-weighted comparison from experienced centers, transcaval TAVR had lower stroke or transient ischemic attack rates than transaxillary access, with similar bleeding and vascular outcomes, though both were less favorable than transfemoral access [21]. Broader alternative-access analyses and network meta-analyses similarly indicate that outcomes depend heavily on patient selection, local expertise, and route-specific hazards [22-24]. Recent systematic reviews of transcaval TAVR report high technical success and acceptable 30-day mortality, bleeding, and vascular event rates, supporting transcaval as a viable option when transfemoral access is contraindicated [25-27].

The scope of transcaval access extends beyond aortic valve implantation. It has enabled thoracic endovascular aortic repair when femoral/iliac arteries were inadequate and has been used for large-bore mechanical circulatory support, including emergent Impella 5.0 delivery in cardiogenic shock [28,29]. These applications are relevant to structural heart programs because patients with severe valve disease, shock, peripheral arterial disease, and prior vascular reconstruction often overlap. Nevertheless, dissemination has been limited by the need for advanced CT interpretation, comfort with catheter electrosurgery, lack of a dedicated approved closure system in many jurisdictions, and the small number of high-volume proctors. Current best practice is therefore to reserve transcaval access for experienced multidisciplinary teams, after systematic comparison with transfemoral facilitation techniques, transaxillary/subclavian, transcarotid, and surgical options. As device profiles shrink and dedicated transcaval systems mature, the role of transcaval access may shift from “last resort” to a deliberate percutaneous alternative for selected structural heart interventions [30].
